newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban Communist Party to hold Congress in October.
newsitem.headline: Cuban Communist Party to hold Congress in October.

text.p: Cuba's ruling Communist Party announced on Wednesday it would hold its Fifth Party Congress in October, saying the meeting would reaffirm the country's determination to stick with a one-party political system.

Party Politburo member Jose Ramon Machado Ventura read the party's formal "call" for the Congress at a ceremony in the central city of Santa Clara to mark the 36th anniversary of the day President Fidel Castro proclaimed the socialist nature of the Cuban Revolution.
Castro and his younger brother, Defence Minister Raul Castro, were at the gathering. Raul Castro made a brief speech following Machado Ventura's announcement.

Machado Ventura made clear the Fifth Party Congress on Oct. 8-10, to be held almost exactly six years after the last congress, would not herald major political change. He also stressed pressure from the United States would not succeed.

He said the congress would "strengthen the unity of the people of Cuba who unhesitatingly confront the savage economic war (the U.S. economic embargo), ideological subversion and pressures and threat of all kinds from the Yankee imperialists".

He added it would "reaffirm the ideological principles in which the Cuban revolutionary process was founded, the irreplaceable role of the single party of the Cuban nation and of the political system."

Raul Castro, Castro's deputy in the party and in government, said the congress was called "to continue defending socialism, to not lose the work of justice created in more than 30 years and to preserve the nation free and sovereign".

The Cuban Communist Party (PCC), the sole legal political party in Cuba and constitutionally the driving force in politics and society, holds its congresses to elect the party leadership and prepare future economic and political strategy.

At the time of the last congress in Oct. 1991, Cuba was sliding rapidly into economic crisis triggered by the collapse of communism in the former Soviet Union and the old East bloc, its former economic allies.
The island of 11 million people is only now starting to emerge from steep economic decline after cautious economic reforms undertaken from 1993.

Machado Ventura said "necessary economic transformations, the natural social wear and tear in these hard years (since the last party congress) and the increased action of the enemy (the United States) have been a tremendous challenge for political-ideological work".

This reflected concern by authorities that the economic changes -- which have included a modest opening to the private sector, the legalisation of dollars and a drive for foreign investment and more tourism -- have had a corrupting influence on revolutionary ideology.
Castro said earlier this month the economic reforms had been undertaken out of necessity and deplored some of their effects, notably what he called "social indiscipline".
Officials reject the notion that the reforms represent the start of a transition to capitalism, saying the state will retain a dominant role in the economy.
